items.prompt: A page creates 1,000 `Cart` instances. How many copies of the `addItem` function exist, and why?
items.answer: One: class methods live on Cart.prototype and are shared by every instance
distractors: 1,000: the class body re-creates every method inside each `new Cart()` call
1,000 at first, until the engine merges the copies into one after the first call
None until called: each instance compiles its own methods lazily on first use
items.explanation: The lesson: methods like addItem and getTotal are shared through the class prototype rather than recreated on every instance, and each instance reaches them through the prototype chain; classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes. (Only `this.items` is per instance.)

items.prompt: `parseUser('{"age": 31}')` is called. The JSON is valid. What does the caller get back?
items.answer: null: the missing-name throw is caught by the same catch that handles bad JSON
distractors: The object { age: 31 }, because the catch only handles JSON.parse syntax errors
An Error thrown to the caller, since a hand-written throw escapes its own try
undefined, because the function stops at the throw before reaching any return
items.explanation: Both failure modes the lesson names (invalid JSON, missing required data) end in the one catch block, which logs the message and returns null.

items.prompt: The Lab 03C `safeParse(json, fallback)` is used for a settings file. What does it give up compared with the lesson's `parseUser`?
items.answer: Any trace of the failure: a corrupt file looks the same as a real fallback value
distractors: Nothing: the optional catch binding still logs the caught error automatically
It rethrows parse errors to the caller, which makes it less safe than parseUser
It cannot parse arrays, because the fallback parameter defaults to null instead
items.explanation: `catch { return fallback; }` swallows the error entirely - it neither logs nor validates - so a corrupt file and a file that genuinely holds the fallback value look identical. parseUser at least logs `error.message` and checks required data.

items.prompt: With the reference `BankAccount`, a fresh account receives `deposit(20)` then `withdraw(50)`. What is `getBalance()`, and what does that reveal about the solution?
items.answer: -30: withdraw subtracts unconditionally, so nothing prevents overdrawing
distractors: 20: withdraw silently ignores any amount larger than the current balance
0: the balance is clamped at zero by the subtraction assignment operator
It throws a RangeError because the balance would otherwise go below zero
items.explanation: The solution only shows the class shape; `this.balance -= amount` has no guard, so the class enforces no business rule against overdrawing (or negative amounts). A real account would validate before mutating.

items.prompt: Why is `import { double } from "./math.js"` better than defining `double` as a global that app.js just uses?
items.answer: The dependency is named in app.js, and math.js's unexported code stays private
distractors: Imported functions run faster, because modules are compiled ahead of time
import copies the function, so later edits to math.js cannot affect app.js
Globals cannot be called across files at all, so an import is the only option
items.explanation: Modules reduce hidden global state and make reuse explicit (the lesson's line under the example): the import names the dependency at the top of app.js, and anything math.js does not export stays out of shared global scope.

items.prompt: Why does `loadPosts` test `response.ok` itself instead of trusting its catch block to see failed requests?
items.answer: fetch rejects only on network failure; a 404 or 500 response still resolves
distractors: The check makes fetch retry the request once before the catch block runs
await throws for 4xx statuses but not 5xx, so the check covers server errors
response.json() would hang on an error status unless ok is checked first
items.explanation: The lesson calls this a common beginner mistake: assuming fetch throws on every failed HTTP status. Without the explicit throw on !response.ok the error path would never run.

items.prompt: A button handler runs `loadPosts(); console.log("after");` without awaiting. When does "after" print relative to the posts appearing?
items.answer: Before them: await suspends only loadPosts, not the calling handler
distractors: After the posts render, because await inside loadPosts blocks the program
Never, since an un-awaited async call cancels the rest of the handler
After the posts render, since console output waits for pending fetches
items.explanation: The lesson: `await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program, so the handler continues as soon as loadPosts hits its first await.

items.prompt: In the Lab 05 solutions, the users endpoint returns 503. What does the #status element finally say?
items.answer: "Error: Status: 503", because the rejected loadUsers lands in showUsers' catch
distractors: "Loaded users.", because loadUsers has no try/catch of its own and cannot fail
"Loading..." forever, because callers cannot see a rejection from another async function
Nothing at all, because the #status element is cleared before the request is sent
items.explanation: loadUsers throws on !response.ok, so its promise rejects; `await loadUsers()` re-throws it inside showUsers' try, whose catch writes the message.

items.prompt: Why does `wait(ms)` build `new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms))` instead of just returning `setTimeout(...)`?
items.answer: setTimeout returns a timer id, which cannot be awaited; the wrapper makes a promise
distractors: setTimeout already returns a promise, and wrapping it only adds proper error handling
The wrapper runs the delay on a separate thread so it cannot block rendering
Without the wrapper the timer fires immediately, because ms would be ignored
items.explanation: The lesson presents it as the promise version of a delay: handing resolve to the timer gives callers a promise that settles when the delay ends, so `.then` / `await` can wait on it.

items.prompt: `app.use(express.json())` is deleted. A client POSTs `{"title":"Ship it"}` with a JSON content type. Does a task get created?
items.answer: No: nothing parses the body, so the handler cannot read req.body.title
distractors: Yes: Express parses JSON bodies by default; the middleware only validates them
Yes, but the title is stored as the raw, unparsed JSON string of the body
No, because express.json() is the call that registers the POST /tasks route
items.explanation: The lesson: express.json() parses JSON request bodies so req.body is usable. Without it req.body is not populated.

items.prompt: In `POST /tasks`, the `return` before `res.status(400)` is removed. A request arrives with title "   ". What goes wrong?
items.answer: The handler runs on: it stores a blank-titled task and tries to respond twice
distractors: Nothing: sending a response automatically ends the route handler's execution
The request hangs, because res.status without return never sends anything
Express rejects the blank title by itself before the route handler even runs
items.explanation: The lesson's order is parse, validate, apply logic, store, respond; `return` is what stops invalid input from reaching the store. Without it the handler keeps going after the 400.

items.prompt: The tasks API is scaled to two instances behind a load balancer, still using `const tasks = []`. A user creates a task, then lists tasks. What can happen?
items.answer: The list may hit the other instance, whose own array never saw the task
distractors: Nothing: both instances share the array, since module variables are host-global
The second request blocks until the first instance replicates its array
The task appears twice in the list, once from each instance's copy of it
items.explanation: The lesson lists the limits of an in-memory array: lost on restart, does not scale across multiple instances. Each instance has its own separate array.

items.prompt: What makes the `isValidEmail` tests short and reliable, according to the lesson?
items.answer: It has one job and no hidden external state, so its output is predictable
distractors: Node's built-in test runner retries failing assertions until they finally pass
strict assert ignores type differences such as true versus "true"
The tests mock the email server, so no network call is ever involved
items.explanation: Pure functions are listed first among the easiest high-value test targets: a given input always produces the same checkable output.

items.prompt: You changed one thing and the error message went away. Per the lesson's workflow, what must you still do before calling the bug fixed?
items.answer: Re-run the original reproduction path, since a vanished symptom is not proof
distractors: Revert the change and try a different one, to confirm it was not just luck
Add a comment explaining the fix, which stands in for re-testing the change
Change the surrounding layers as well, so the same class of bug cannot recur
items.explanation: Steps 5 and 6: fix one thing at a time, then re-test the original reproduction path. The symptom vanishing does not show the reported behavior is now correct.

items.front: The tasks API assigns `id: Date.now()`. Two POSTs land within the same millisecond. What breaks later?
items.back: Both tasks get the same id, so a DELETE or PATCH by id (Labs 07A/07B) hits the wrong task or both. Use a counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or a database key.

items.front: Both lesson tests pass, yet `isValidEmail("@.")` returns what — and what does that say about the two tests?
items.back: true: it only checks that "@" and "." appear somewhere. Two happy/sad examples did not pin down the rule; add edge cases (missing local part, dot before @).

items.front:
`loadPosts` renders with `list.innerHTML = posts.map(post => `
  • ${post.title}
    • `)`. A post title contains ``. What happens?
items.back: The markup is parsed and the handler runs (XSS). Build elements and set textContent for API data, or escape it, instead of interpolating into innerHTML.

items.front: A caller of `parseUser` gets null. Can it tell whether the input was broken JSON or a user without a name?
items.back: No: both failures go through one catch and return null; only the console log differs. Return a result with a reason, or throw distinct errors, when callers must react differently.
